oil.summary: Crude pulled back sharply on Friday after Thursday's geopolitical spike drove Brent briefly past $100/bbl — the session high cited across multiple wire reports. WTI settled around $90.37 (-1.91%) and Brent at $98.05 (-2.62%), with RBOB gasoline cratering 6.52% and heating oil off 4.88%, suggesting some profit-taking and demand-side anxiety after a violent run-up. The underlying supply disruption narrative remains acute: Houthi strikes on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, IRGC interceptions of three tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, and Hormuz crossings falling to their lowest level since May 7 have collectively tightened the physical market. Saudi Red Sea crude exports have sunk 41% since their March peak, ADNOC continues tendering despite the risks, and China is pivoting to Russian and Iranian barrels as Gulf flows falter — though Russian supply is itself increasingly constrained.
drivers: Strait of Hormuz near-blockade: only one tanker transit on Thursday; IRGC intercepted three vessels mid-week
Houthi strikes on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea cut Saudi Red Sea crude exports 41% from March peak
Post-spike profit-taking dragged WTI/Brent lower on the day despite monthly gains of ~29-33%

gas.summary: The Henry Hub/TTF divergence widened further on Friday. Henry Hub edged down 0.48% to $2.902/MMBtu, continuing a roughly 10% monthly slide that reflects ample domestic U.S. supply; a new Baker Hughes rig count showed total U.S. oil and gas active rigs fell again this week despite near-$100 crude. European TTF surged 2.43% to €63.405/MWh, up an extraordinary 55% over the past month, driven by Middle East supply anxiety, rerouting pressure on LNG flows, and the continuing Ukraine conflict. The EU agreed a new sanctions deal that keeps Russian gas cargoes exempt for now, a political compromise that limits near-term TTF upside but has not stopped the rally. A separate report noted Russia's largest Black Sea oil terminal went quiet following drone attacks that also hit the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal nearby.
drivers: TTF +55% on the month as Middle East conflict threatens LNG re-routing and European supply security
Henry Hub soft (-9.9% monthly) on domestic oversupply; U.S. rig count fell again per Baker Hughes
EU sanctions exemption for Russian gas cargoes limits immediate supply shock but war risk premium persists

power.summary: News flow for the power and carbon sector is thin today. EU carbon EUAs dipped modestly, settling at $79.03/EUA (-0.73% on the day) but still up ~5% on the week and ~3.5% on the month, tracking the broader energy complex without a strong independent catalyst. TTF's 2.43% daily gain — the dominant input cost for European gas-fired generation — adds upward pressure to power prices. On the geopolitical side, a Russian attack cut power to roughly 150,000 households in northern Ukraine, and Kyiv struck Russian missile and oil facilities in retaliation. The UK announced nearly 300 new sanctions targeting Russian entities including Transneft. U.S. LNG dominance was highlighted in a separate report noting the U.S. supplied approximately 1.10 trillion cubic feet of the ~1.2 trillion cubic feet growth in global LNG exports during 2025.
drivers: TTF at €63.40/MWh (+2.43%) lifts European gas-fired generation costs, indirectly pressuring power prices
Russian strike cuts power to ~150,000 in northern Ukraine; UK imposes new sanctions on Transneft
EUA carbon slipped 0.73% on the day; headline flow is limited and sector-specific catalysts are sparse
